Language-model representations correlate with human sentence-processing effort, but the best-aligned layers depend on the kind of reading. For naturalistic reading, earlier layers model processing behavior; for syntactically challenging ambiguity, later layers better estimate human effort, though they still underestimate it [1].

Other evidence links model signals to human brain responses: language-model features and surprisal predict neural responses, with general-purpose representation features contributing beyond surprisal in some regions [2]. Reading-time studies also find that model surprisal tracks human behavior and that long-range coreference can improve its predictions [4].
